description: Annotate Markdown or diffs in the terminal: select, comment, looks-good, delete; send the review to your agent.

latest_release.name: v0.12.1
latest_release.body:
## Fix

- **Rex: Send reaches the agent again.** Since Rex server 0.1.0-preview.23, a new Rex terminal sets `REX_BLOCK` and no longer `REX_SESSION`. A review opened in Rex then found no agent to send to and copied the feedback to the clipboard instead. The session is now found from `REX_BLOCK`. Thanks @micmcg for the report and the fix (#212, #213).
- If a Rex review cannot reach its agent, Send now says so (`claude · not found`, with the reason) instead of copying silently, and the notes stay unsent.
- A reopened code review whose notes were only copied says `Copied ✓`, not `Sent ✓`.

If you sent notes from a Rex review with 0.12.0 or earlier and they never arrived: reopen the review and press `R` to send them all again.

## What's Changed
* fix(rex): find the session from REX_BLOCK when REX_SESSION is unset by @micmcg in https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui/pull/213
* release: 0.12.1 by @backnotprop in https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui/pull/214

## New Contributors
* @micmcg made their first contribution in https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui/pull/213

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui/compare/v0.12.0...v0.12.1

detail.readme: Annotate Markdown in the terminal. Select text, leave a 💬 comment, mark it 👍 looks good or ✗ delete, and hand the review to a coding agent as numbered feedback. One static binary, no runtime. Rust + ratatui. [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/plannotator-tui?style=flat-square)](https://crates.io/crates/plannotator-tui) [![release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/plannotator/plannotator-tui?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui/releases) [![ci](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/plannotator/plannotator-tui/post-merge.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=main)](https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui/actions/workflows/post-merge.yml) ```text Send 2 to claude in w1:p1 ▸ Herdr plugins are shareable, executable workflow packages. A plugin can be a Bash script, JavaScript app, Lua script, Rust ▍ binary, or any other argv command your machine can run. Herdr ╭ 💬 8d3e8 ────────────────╮ ▍ owns the host surface: installation, manifest validation, │ Say which parts the │ keybindings, terminal panes, events, invocation context, and │ plugin can override. │ socket access. The plugin owns its implementation language, ╰──────────────────────────╯ dependencies, files, and durable state. 👍 looks good (a) 💬 comment (c) ✗ delete (d) ▍ Plugins exist so Herdr can stay lean. The core stays focused on ╭ 👍 25300 ────────────────╮ ▍ terminal workspaces, panes, agents, and a stable CLI/socket API. │ looks good │ ▍ Plugins turn that existing extension surface into reusable ╰──────────────────────────╯ ▍ workflows that people can build, install, and share without ▍ adding every workflow to Herdr itself. plugins.md · 2 annotations · selected 36 chars a looks good · c comment · d delete · esc clear ``` Watch it inside Herdr: [demo](https://x.com/plannotator/status/2093419561077154287). ## Install ```sh brew trust plannotator/tap && brew install plannotator/tap/plannotator-tui # macOS, Linux cargo install plannotator-tui # anywhere with Rust ``` Homebrew 6 asks you to trust a third-party tap once before installing from it. Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows are on the [releases page](https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui/releases). On x86_64 Linux, choose `plannotator-tui-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` if the GNU binary reports a missing `GLIBC_*` version, or if you use Alpine. This static musl build does not require system glibc or a local Rust toolchain. Existing GNU/Linux binaries remain available. Verify your download against `SHA256SUMS` from the same release, make it executable, and put it on your `PATH` as `plannotator-tui`. ## Use ```sh plannotator-tui docs/plan.md # one file plannotator-tui docs # a folder: file tree on the left, counts per file plannotator-tui last # your coding agent's recent replies, pick one, annotate it ``` Drag with the mouse (or `v`, move, then `Enter`) to select, then `a` 👍 · `c` 💬 · `d` ✗. `E` copies the feedback to the clipboard as numbered annotations (`# Annotations on plan.md`, `## Annotation 1 (line 12)`, …), or, when an agent is within reach, first asks which agent to send to (see [Choosing the agent](#choosing-the-agent)). Every annotation is saved as JSON the moment you make it; `q` closes. `I` attaches a local image to the selected note (in the notes, or the selected block's note in the document): type, paste or drop its path, then `Enter`. Quoted, `~` and `file://` paths work; a relative path starts at the document's folder. PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP and SVG files are accepted. The feedback lists each one as `Image: /absolute/path.png` under its note, so the agent opens it from your disk; nothing is copied or uploaded. `D` removes the last image added. Adding or removing an image makes a sent note pending again. Copies go to the clipboard as OSC 52, which is the terminal you are looking at, so on Herdr 0.9.0 they reach your own machine even when the app runs on a remote server; Herdr Annotate's global `copy-context` and `copy-archive` actions do not, because they run outside a pane. On an agent's reply, `S` sends the feedback and closes the window in one key, the same as `q` then `y`. `E` still sends and leaves the window open. When the agent is at a dialog the window stays open and the footer says why; press `S` again to retry. With nothing to send, or with a review the agent already has, `S` closes like `q`. File and folder reviews have no `S`; they finish with `F`. For file and folder reviews, `E` sends only new or edited annotations. Send A and B, then add C: the next send includes just C. Sent notes stay visible with a marker; editing one makes it pending again, including after a restart. `R` **Resend all** includes every active note. With nothing pending, `E` reports “nothing new to send” and the button reads `Sent ✓ ▸ claude in w1:p2` (`Copied ✓` for the clipboard) until there is a new note. When the agent is at a dialog it reads `claude in w1:p2 at a dialog · retry (E)`. A failed send keeps the notes pending for retry. `F` **Finish review** archives sent, unchanged notes and leaves pending ones in place. `U` undoes the last finish during this session. `H` opens the archive, where Enter or a click restores a note even after reopening the app. Restoring keeps its original id and sent status. The archive is stored with the annotations and works even when feedback history is turned off. The header holds the send button and a `Review ▾ (m)` button whose menu lists these four actions with live counts (`R` resend all · 3 sent, `F` finish review · archive 3 sent, `U` undo finish, `H` archive · 2 notes); rows with nothing to act on are dimmed. The keys also work without opening the menu. | Where | Keys | |---|---| | anywhere | `Tab` cycle tree · document · notes; `z` hide or show the notes; `E` send; `P` choose the agent to send to; `t` tree; `r` reload; `o` open the file in `$EDITOR`; `q` quit | | reply review | `S` send and close | | gated review | `A` approve; `E` send and finish; `q` dismiss | | document | `j`/`k` block; `c` comment on the block; `a` looks good; `d` delete; `x` clear its annotations; `X` clear every annotation on the document, after a `y`; `v` select with `hjkl` `w` `b` `e` `0` `$`, then `a`, `c` or `d` to act on it, `y` to copy it, or `Enter` for the toolbar; `V` select whole rows; `i` move the cursor with those keys first, then `v` to select from there; `I`/`D` attach or remove an image on the block's note; `/` search the text, then `n`/`N` next/previous match | | toolbar | `a` looks good · `c` comment · `d` delete · `y` copy · `Esc` | | comment box | `Enter` save; `Shift+Enter`, `Alt+Enter` or `Ctrl+J` new line; `↑`/`↓` move by display row; `Ctrl+←`/`Ctrl+→`, `Alt+←`/`Alt+→` or `Alt+B`/`Alt+F` jump by word; `Ctrl+A`/`Ctrl+E` line start/end; `Ctrl+W`, `Alt+Backspace` or `Ctrl+Backspace` delete the previous word; `Alt+D` or `Ctrl+Delete` delete the next word; `Ctrl+U`/`Ctrl+K` delete to line start/end; `Esc` cancel, asking first if the text changed | | notes | `j`/`k`; `e` edit; `x` remove; `I` attach an image, `D` remove the last; click a bubble | | file/folder review | `E` send new · `m` review menu (`R` resend all · `F` finish review · `U` undo · `H` archive) | | folder review | `Ctrl+P` open a file by name, including in collapsed folders: type, `↑`/`↓` or click, `Enter`, `Esc` | | tree | `j`/`k`; `Enter` open; `.` show/hide dot-prefixed entries (`.agents/`, `.github/`); `E` sends new notes across all reviewed files, including collapsed folders | | code review | drag with the mouse or `v` select, `v` again to end; `c` comment; `y` copy the selected lines; `s` suggest code; `C` note on the file; `M` note on the whole change; `o`/`O` whole file now/before; `d` go to definition, `ctrl+o`/`ctrl+i` back/forward; `]`/`[` hunk; `n`/`N` file; `x` viewed; `ctrl+n` next not viewed; `h`/`l` old/new side; `u` split/unified; `w` wrap; `W` hide or show whitespace-only changes; `(`/`)` move the line between the sides (or drag it); `,` diff settings; `f` the file list; `/` filter files by name; `t` filter by kind; `H` hide viewed files; `<`/`>` list width; `{`/`}` notes width (or drag the line between the panes); `z` hide or show the notes; `r` read the diff again (the footer says when it changed on disk); `?` keys | These are the defaults; every key can be rebound under `[keys]` (see [Keys](#keys)). The notes rail on the right appears with a document's first note: a document or diff without notes gets every column. In the code review a saved note never opens it, so the diff keeps its width; there it shows when the review opens with notes, and `z` or `Tab` opens it. `z` closes it, and it stays closed until `z` or `Tab` opens it again: a new note, a wider window, another file or a reload leave it closed, and the header and footer still count the notes, whose marks stay in the text. The next session starts the way you left it. `notes_rail` in the config file's `[ui]` table changes how it starts; it is described with the other `[ui]` settings. ### Approval gate When a script or an agent must know whether you signed off, add `--gate`. The review gains an **Approve** action (`A`, and an `Approve (A)` button on the header's edge) beside Send and quit, and ends with one decision: Approve is `approved`, a successful Send is `annotated`, and quitting is `dismissed`. Notes you have not sent yet ride along with an approval (`Approve with 2 notes (A)`). Without `--gate` nothing changes. ```sh plannotator-tui docs/plan.md --gate # prints the outcome when you finish plannotator-tui docs/plan.md --gate --json --require-approval --result-file /tmp/plan-decision.json ``` The output is the one `plannotator annotate --gate` prints. Plain `--gate` prints `The user approved.`, the approved-with-notes message (the notes plus the file they are about), the feedback, or nothing for a dismissal. `--json` prints one line instead, `{"decision":"approved|annotated|dismissed","feedback":"…"}`; `feedback` is absent from a bare approval and a dismissal, and the line also carries `annotationCount` and the reviewed `target`. `--json` without `--gate` decides between `annotated` and `dismissed` only. For a gate a script can trust, add either or both strict flags (they need `--gate --json`): - `--require-approval` exits 0 only on approval and 1 on `annotated` or `dismissed`. - `--result-file ` also writes `{"decision":…,"feedback":…}` to ``, atomically, and never over an existing file: the folder must exist and the file must not. A relative path starts at the current directory. Under a strict flag a failure of the gate itself (a bad flag, a missing file, a result file that cannot be written) exits 2, never 1. The review draws on stdout, so a gated review refuses to start when stdout is not a terminal: read the decision from `--result-file` rather than capturing stdout. Each decision is also added to the feedback archive as `approved`, `approved-with-notes`, `feedback` or `dismissed`. `o` hands the terminal to `$VISUAL` (or `$EDITOR`, which may carry flags such as `code -w`) on the open file, at the current line for vim, nvim, nano, helix, emacs, micro and kak. When the editor exits the viewer comes back and, if the file changed, reloads it as `r` does so notes re-anchor. A GUI editor without its wait flag returns at once; save later and the footer says the file changed. Reply and terminal reviews have no file, so `o` does nothing there. Hidden folders are out of the tree until `.` asks for them, and `.git`, `.hg`, `.svn`, `.jj`, `.cache`, `.direnv`, `.venv`, `venv`, `__pycache__`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `target`, `build`, `dist` and `out` stay out either way — none of them is read at all. Showing or hiding is a view choice: notes recorded for a file inside a hidden folder are part of the review and are sent whether or not its folder is listed. `Ctrl+P` matches file names, not contents, ignoring case and allowing gaps (`prd` finds `product-requirements.md`). Results show the path within the folder, so files with the same name are told apart, and opening one expands the tree down to it. It follows the tree's hidden-entries setting and skips the same folders the tree does. ### Search `/` opens a search line at the bottom of the document. Every match is highlighted as you type, and the cursor moves to the first one at or after it; the footer counts them (`3/17`). `Enter` keeps the search and closes the line, `Esc` closes it and puts the view back. `n` and `N` then go to the next and previous match, wrapping at either end, and `Esc` clears the highlights. An empty search clears them too. A search is plain text, not a pattern, and ignores case unless it has a capital letter. It matches the text as shown: Markdown markup is invisible to it, and a match can run across a wrapped line, inside a table cell or a list item. It does not cross a hard line break or run from one list item or table row into the next. The cursor lands on the match, so `v` selects from it. A search moves only the cursor and the view: a waiting selection and every note stay as they were. In a folder review a search covers the open file only; opening another file drops it. ## Code review ```sh plannotator-tui review # uncommitted changes in this repository plannotator-tui review --staged # only what is staged plannotator-tui review --unstaged # only what is not staged yet (untracked files too) plannotator-tui review --pick # pick: uncommitted, unstaged, staged, the branch, a commit plannotator-tui review --base main # everything since this branch left main plannotator-tui review --commit 1a2b3c # one commit plannotator-tui review ../other-repo # another repository plannotator-tui review 123 # pull request #123 of this repository (also #123) plannotator-tui review https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123 ``` `review` opens a git diff. With nothing uncommitted (and nothing on the branch), it opens the [change picker](#pick-what-to-review) instead, so you can pick the commit the agent just made; when its output is not a terminal it fails as before. Move with `j`/`k`, `]`/`[` for the next or previous hunk, and `n`/`N` for the next or previous file. `h` and `l` go to the old and new side of a line. `v` starts a selection and a second `v` ends it. Then: - `c` writes a comment on the lines. - `s` writes a suggestion: the box opens with the new lines, so you edit the code you want. - `C` writes a note on the whole file. - `M` writes a note on the whole change (also the first row of the Review menu). It sits at the top of the rail under **Whole change**, and the agent gets it first, under `## Global comments`, as the browser sends its global comments. The comment box opens right under the lines, or above them when they are at the bottom of the diff. In a split diff it opens over the side the lines are on, wherever you dragged the line between the sides; a side narrower than the box gets the box from its outer edge. It covers none of the lines while there is room, and they stay shaded while you type. A note on a file opens under the file's heading. A note on the whole change opens in the middle, and editing a note from the rail opens the box under the note's lines. The box grows as you type, up to eight lines, and then scrolls. Opening, typing, saving or `Esc` never scrolls the diff or moves the cursor. While the box is open, a click on its text moves the text cursor there. A click anywhere else and the wheel do nothing, so a stray click never loses what you typed: the header's switches and `Settings` button and the line between the sides stay as they are, and `,`, `u`, `w`, `W`, `(` and `)` are text in the box. The mouse works too. The wheel scrolls the diff, the file list or the notes under the pointer. A click puts the cursor on a line, on the old or new side you clicked; a click on a file in the file list goes to that file, a click on a folder opens or closes it, and a click on a note selects it and shows its lines. The Send and `Review ▾` buttons in the header are clickable. Drag over lines to select them: a selection is whole lines on the side where the drag started, as in the browser's code review, and the lines are shaded while you drag. Drag past the top or bottom of the diff to scroll. When you let go, a small toolbar next to the lines offers `💬 comment` and `✎ suggest` (click it, or press `c` or `s`), and the note is anchored on exactly those lines, with their code quoted for the agent. `Esc` clears the selection. Drag works the same in the whole-file view. Shift-click grows a selection to the clicked line, from the line the drag started on. A selection stays inside the hunk it started in, as GitHub's multi-line comments do: a drag or a `v` selection stops at the hunk's first or last line. A key, a second click, or the window losing focus before you let go drops the drag, and its shading with it. Drag the line between the file list and the diff, or between the diff and the notes, to make the list or the notes wider or narrower; the line lights up under the pointer and while you drag it. `<`/`>` do the same for the list and `{`/`}` for the notes, four columns at a time. The width you set stays for the rest of the review, through filters and `r`, and the diff always keeps room to show its code; a window made narrower for a while draws the panes narrower and gives them the width you set back when it widens. Double-click the line (two clicks on one cell, without moving) to let the list or the notes fit themselves again. Notes appear in the rail on the right, grouped by file, and a mark in the diff shows their lines. Sent notes get a dimmer mark. `Tab` moves to the rail; `j`/`k` there moves to a note and the diff moves with it; `e` edits and `x` removes it. The rail shows when the review opens with notes. Saving a note never opens it, so the diff stays where it was: the note's lines get their mark, the footer says `note saved` and where the notes are (`notes hidden: z shows them`), and the header's Send counts it. `z` or `Tab` opens the rail, and `z` closes it and gives the diff its columns. Closed, it stays closed, as in a document review. `E` sends the new notes, `S` sends them and closes, and `P` picks the agent to send to. Sends go to the same place a document review's do (Herdr pane, Rex, Pi or the clipboard, or the agent you choose when nothing named one; see [Choosing the agent](#choosing-the-agent)), and are kept in the feedback archive. `q` asks first when notes are unsent. `m` opens the Review menu: `M` comment on the whole change, `R` resend all, `F` finish review, `U` undo. `U` also brings back the last note removed in this session, where it was. `o` shows the whole file under the cursor as it is now, scrolled to the same line; `O` shows it as it was before the change (the base), at the matching old line. The header says `Whole file · new` or `Whole file · base (1a2b3c4)`, a bar in the gutter marks the lines the change added (or removed), and `]`/`[` move between them. `n`/`N` go to the next or previous file, and `o`, `O` or `Esc` go back to the diff where you left it. `c` in the current file writes an ordinary diff note when the diff shows those lines; on lines outside every hunk it writes a note **not in the diff**, which the rail lists under its own heading and the agent gets with the code quoted, as the browser sends one. `Enter` on such a note in the rail opens the whole file at its lines. The base is read-only for notes. Files over 5 MiB, binary files, an added file's base and a deleted file's current version are not shown; the view says which. `d` goes to the definition of a word on the cursor's line, in the diff or the whole file. With several identifiers on the line, a small list asks which (`1`-`9` or `Enter`). The search (`git grep`, the same patterns and ranking as the browser's code navigation) runs in the background on the side you are on: the new side searches the reviewed version, the old side and the base view search the base; in a pull request it reads the PR's commits, also from the cache repository. One clear answer is jumped to: in the diff when it shows that line, otherwise in the whole file. Several are listed with `path:line`, definition or use, and the line; `Enter` goes, `Esc` closes. `ctrl+o` goes back to where you jumped from and `ctrl+i` forward again (in terminals that tell `ctrl+i` from Tab). `r` reads the diff again after you or the agent change files. Notes follow their lines. The review checks for changes by itself every few seconds (a `git status` and the times of the changed files; never while you type, less often in a large repository), and the footer then says `the diff changed on disk · r refreshes`. It never reloads by itself. Commit and pull request reviews have nothing on disk to check. A note whose lines changed goes to the **Outdated** group at the end of the rail; it is still sent, marked as outdated. `u` switches between split and unified view, `w` wraps long lines and `?` shows every key. The header shows the layout as a switch, `Split Unified` with the one in force lit, and a `Wrap` switch beside it; a click on either does what `u` or `w` does. In a split diff, drag the line between the old and the new side to give one side more of the width, or press `(` and `)`; a double click on the line makes the sides even again. Each side keeps at least 20 columns. `,` (or the header's `Settings` button) opens the diff settings: layout, split ratio, wrap, notes, line numbers, whitespace, tab width, changed text, colours and background, each with its value. `↑`/`↓` pick one, `←`/`→` change it, `enter` or `space` moves it on (and evens the split ratio), a click on a row does the same, and `esc` closes the menu. Every change applies at once and is remembered for the next review, however you made it (the menu, the switches, a key or a drag); the menu's last row, **Reset to defaults**, forgets those choices and goes back to [`[review]`](#how-diffs-open) in the config file, else the defaults. A narrow header gives up the key hints first, then the `Wrap` switch, the `Settings` button and the `Review` button, and keeps the layout switch longest (as `S U` when it must). The settings' **Notes** row draws the notes in the diff, as a pull request's comments sit in its diff: `panel` (the default) keeps them in the notes panel only, `inline` draws each in a box under the last line it is about, and `both` does both. A box sits over its side of a split diff (across both sides when that side is too narrow), several on one line stack in the order they were made, and a note on the whole file sits under the file's heading. The box shows the note's kind and lines, its author when it is not you, `sent` once sent, and up to six lines of its text (a suggestion's code as `-`/`+` lines); `… enter for more` says there is more. The cursor stops once on each box: `enter` or `e` opens the note in the comment box over it, `delete` removes it (`U` brings it back), `c` or `s` there writes another note on the same lines, under it, and a click on a box picks its note (in the panel too). A drag selects code only, and boxes never move the line you are on: a note saved on the pane's last row says `note saved · below, ↓ shows it`. A pane under 10 rows shows no boxes (`pane too small for inline notes`). Notes on the whole change, and notes whose lines the diff does not show now (outdated, in a hunk hidden with `W`, in a filtered-out file), get no box: the footer counts them (`2 notes not shown inline · z`) and the panel lists them. With `inline` the panel starts away whatever notes there are; `z` opens it for the session. The whole-file view (`o`/`O`) keeps its notes in the panel. The changed files are listed left of the diff as a folder tree. A chain of folders with one folder each is one row (`crates/app/src/`), and the list is as wide as its names need, up to two fifths of the screen. A name that does not fit is cut in the middle, so its end and extension stay readable; the diff heading shows the whole path. `<` and `>` make the list narrower or wider. Where there is no room for it (80 columns beside the notes) it hides, and `f` opens it, with the notes making way. In the list, `j`/`k` move and show each file, `enter` goes to it, `h`/`l` close and open folders, and `f` closes the list. `/` filters the files by name: every word you type must be in the path (`review test`), and the list follows each key. `enter` hands the filter to the diff, which then shows only those files, so `n`/`N`, `]`/`[` and `ctrl+n` move among them. `esc` clears it. `t` opens the kinds: code, tests, docs, config, generated and other, each with how many files of it the change has. Space turns a kind on or off, `enter` shows that kind alone. `H` hides the files you have marked viewed. The list's heading shows `Files · 12 of 340` and the filter while one is on. Notes are never hidden: the rail keeps them, Send sends them all, and the list says how many unsent notes are in hidden files. The kinds follow the browser's rules for tests and generated files: test folders (`tests/`, `__tests__/`, `spec/`, `fixtures/`, `src/androidTest/`, `Acme.Tests/`), test names (`*.test.ts`, `*.spec.js`, `*_test.go`, `test_*.py`, `*.snap`, `*.stories.tsx`), and generated files (lockfiles, `*.min.js`, `*.map`). Here `*.pb.go`, `*.g.dart`, `vendor/`, `node_modules/` and `dist/` are generated too. Docs are prose (`*.md`, `*.rst`, `*.txt`, `README`, `LICENSE`, `docs/`); config is data and build files (`*.json`, `*.yaml`, `*.toml`, dotfiles, `Dockerfile`, `Makefile`, `*.config.ts`); code is source by extension; the rest is other. `x` marks the file under the cursor viewed, and `x` again unmarks it. The header counts them (`3/12 viewed`), the file list ticks viewed files and dims them, and `ctrl+n` goes to the next file you have not viewed. Marks are saved in the browser app's own format under the data folder (`review-progress/`), so a review started in the browser continues here and the other way round. A mark stops counting once its file changes. Set `PLANNOTATOR_REVIEW_PROGRESS=0` to keep marks for the session only. See [docs/spec-review-progress.md](docs/spec-review-progress.md). ### Pick what to review `plannotator-tui review --pick`, or `p` (`pick-changes`) in a review, opens the change picker. Its rows never move: ``` Uncommitted (no changes) Unstaged (no changes) Staged (no changes) Branch vs origin/main +120 −30 · 9 files 2h ▸ a1b2c3d feat: login redirect +12 −3 · 4 files 5m Ada 2 unsent 9f8e7d6 fix: session timeout +4 −1 · 1 file 1d Ada …the last 20 commits, newest first more… ``` The branch row is there when its base (`origin/HEAD`) is known and the branch has moved past it. A row with nothing in it is dimmed and says `(no changes)`; `2 unsent` counts notes saved on that row's review and not sent yet, and `open` marks the review you came from. The cursor starts on the first row with changes, so when the agent has committed and the tree is clean, it is on that commit and the footer says `No uncommitted changes · pick a commit below`. Over a review, the cursor starts on that review's row. The commits show at once; the sizes fill in from the background, the rows on screen first, with `…` until then. At most two git commands run for them at a time; `r`, a choice or closing the picker stops the ones running, and quitting leaves no git command or index copy behind. They run off the terminal: one that asks for input there (a clean filter or credential helper) is stopped and its row says `(needs the terminal)`. Before any screen opens, git runs as before, so such a prompt shows and can be answered. `j`/`k`, `g`/`G` and `PageUp`/`PageDown` move, `enter` (or a click) reviews the row and `more…` lists 20 older commits; the wheel scrolls. `r` lists the commits and counts the changes again. `?` shows these keys and `q` quits. Over a review, `esc` or `p` goes back to it. A review you pick takes the delivery target, the agent `P` chose, the diff settings and the keys of the one before; notes you had not sent stay saved on their own review, and the footer says so (`2 unsent notes kept on Uncommitted`). Quitting asks first while notes are unsent on any review you opened this session, and names them apart from the review's own (`y send these to … · 1 more unsent on Commit 2efc81b (esc go to it) · n quit`); `esc` there opens the picker on that review. A review gone from the branch since (a commit amended away) is named once: its notes are kept, and quitting does not ask about them again. Choosing the row of the review you are in goes back to it as it was. Each row reviews exactly that diff: an empty one only says so, and one that cannot open (a patch over 8 MiB, say) says why and the picker stays; a commit gone since the list was read says to press `r`. A commit row is the diff `--commit` shows: a merge commit against its first parent. A commit that changes no lines (binary files, renames) shows its file count only. Unstaged and Uncommitted are two reviews with notes of their own, as `--unstaged` and a bare `review` are. A bare `review` in a repository with no commits yet still fails with `No uncommitted changes`; `--pick` opens the picker there anyway. `--pick` takes a folder, so a number after it is refused rather than read as a pull request: give a folder named only by digits as `./123`. ### Pull requests `review` with a pull request link, a number or `#123` (also `--pr PR`) reviews what GitHub shows for that pull request: its head commit against where it left its base branch. It uses your `gh` login (install the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com) and run `gh auth login`). A number is looked up in the GitHub repository of the folder you run it in; a link works from any folder. A folder whose name is only digits is `./123`. The pull request's commits are fetched into your clone when you run it inside one (any remote naming the PR's repository), as the private ref `refs/plannotator-tui/pull//head`. Your branch, index and working files are not touched. Outside a clone of that repository, they are fetched into a cache repository under the data folder (`clients/plannotator-tui/pulls///.git`); the first review of a repository there downloads its history once. The header shows `PR #123 · title · base ← head`. `r` looks the pull request up again and fetches new pushes; notes follow their lines as they do for local changes. Notes are saved once per pull request, whichever clone you open it from. Send goes to the agent as for any review, with the browser's pull request header (`# PR Review: owner/repo#123`, the title, the branches and the link). Nothing is posted to GitHub. A Pi session can leave notes on the diff too (see [Pi](#pi)). Notes are saved with the other annotations, one record per repository and scope. Code review is not available on Windows yet. ## Inside Herdr Install [Herdr Annotate](https://github.com/plannotator/herdr-annotate); it bundles this binary, opens it in a pane with `prefix+o` (folder) or `prefix+shift+o` (agent's last reply), and the header button sends the review straight back to the agent as its next message: `Send 3 new ▸ claude in w1:p2 (E)`. Ctrl-clicking a `file://…md` link opens it in Annotate only if you install the add-on: `herdr plugin install plannotator/herdr-annotate/links`. Folder reviews show `Send 3 new across 2 files` and send one combined feedback message. ```toml # ~/.config/plannotator-tui/config.toml [herdr] placement = "overlay" # overlay (full tab, default) | split | popup ``` `plannotator-tui herdr open plan.md --gate [--result-file ]` opens a gated review. Approve sends the agent `The user approved.` (or the approved-with-notes message), Send sends the numbered feedback as usual, and quitting sends nothing; the window closes on any of the three. With `--result-file` the pane also writes the decision JSON there. The command returns as soon as the pane opens, so a script waits for the file. `plannotator-tui herdr last --newest` opens the agent's newest reply without asking which one; without the flag the picker comes first, as it always has. `plannotator-tui herdr terminal [--lines N]` opens the focused pane's recent output (the last 200 lines by default; Herdr caps a read at 1000) as a transient review, shown verbatim in one code block. Send goes to the agent in that pane, as it does for a reply; a pane with no agent copies instead. `--print` writes the document to stdout instead of opening a pane. Herdr Annotate ships it as the `annotate.terminal` action with no default key. `plannotator-tui herdr review [--staged | --unstaged | --base REF | --commit SHA | PR | --pick]` opens a [code review](#code-review) of the focused pane's git repository (else the workspace's folder) in a pane. Send goes to the agent in that pane. A folder that is not in a repository, or a scope you named with no changes to review, fails before any pane opens; with no scope and nothing to review, the pane opens the [change picker](#pick-what-to-review). `--pick` opens the picker straight away: the launcher only checks the folder is in a repository. The development manifest has them as the `review` and `review-pick` actions with no default key, on macOS and Linux (Herdr manifests cannot declare keys; bind one in Herdr). A Claude Code session is looked up in `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, else `~/.claude`. An agent's own `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` doesn't reach a pane Herdr opens, so if you run several profiles, list them to have them searched for a session Herdr identifies by id: ```toml [last] claude_profile_dirs = ["~/.claude-max", "~/.claude-work"] ``` Finding a session by pid or folder still uses only the first two. `plannotator-tui config` prints the file's path and the values in effect. The `herdr/` directory in this repo is the development manifest; users should install Herdr Annotate. The same file chooses the theme: ```toml [ui] theme = "auto" # auto (ask the terminal, default) | light | dark ``` On `auto` the viewer asks the terminal for its background colour once at startup and uses a light palette when it finds one; a terminal that does not answer keeps the dark palette it has always used. The question costs one round trip before the screen is drawn, and a key pressed into that window is read along with the reply and lost, so set the theme outright if you habitually type ahead. `light` and `dark` skip the question, and `PLANNOTATOR_TUI_THEME=light|dark` does the same for one run — the variable wins over the file, and `plannotator-tui config` prints whichever is in effect. Only the backgrounds plannotator-tui paints itself change; the document keeps your terminal's own colours either way. `[colors]` replaces individual roles of whichever palette is in force; a role left out keeps its light or dark value. A colour is a name (`yellow`, `light-cyan`), a 256-colour index (`238`, quoted or not) or `#rrggbb`. An unknown role or colour is an error that names it, and `plannotator-tui config` prints the roles you set. Every role, with the dark palette's values (apart from `selection`, which is reverse video by default): ```toml [colors] accent = "cyan" # focused borders and gutter, the open file, menu and picker frames heading = "cyan" # every heading level comment = "yellow" # comment titles, the compose box, annotated rows in the gutter looks-good = "green" delete = "red" # also the struck-through text comment-bg = "58" # the tint under commented text looks-good-bg = "22" # the tint under looks-good text block = "236" # the focused block and the focused tree row toolbar = "238" # the floating toolbar and the idle header buttons; 253 on light cursor = "240" # the keyboard cursor cell selection = "#45475a" # a character selection, a picker row, a menu row code = "light-yellow" # inline code, and fenced code without a bundled grammar; 94 on light code-keyword = "magenta" # fenced code with a known language: keywords code-string = "green" # 28 on the light palette code-number = "yellow" # numbers and constants; 130 on light code-function = "blue" code-type = "cyan" # 30 on light code-comment = "dark-gray" # comments (italic), the bar beside code and its language label search = "24" # every match of a document search search-current = "208" # the match the cursor is on (black text by default); 214 on light ``` `cursor`, `selection`, `search` and `search-current` become plain backgrounds when set: the text on them keeps the terminal's colour. The text on the header buttons and the floating toolbar is not a role: each theme picks it from the 256-colour table so that it reads at 4.5:1 or more on the default toolbar grey. A `toolbar` colour far from that grey can make it harder to read. The document's text sits in a reading column, centred in the columns the tree and the notes leave, and `[ui]` sizes it and the app around it: ```toml [ui] doc_width = 80 # the reading column, in columns; 0 lets the text fill the pane max_width = 160 # center the whole app in this many columns horizontal_margin = 2 # blank columns on each side ``` `doc_width` defaults to `80`; `max_width` and `horizontal_margin` default to `0`, which fills the terminal. `<` and `>` narrow and widen the column by eight for the session. The margin and `max_width` yield before the app drops below 80 columns, so a narrow pane keeps its notes rail; a narrow pane also lets the document shrink below `doc_width`. Fenced code is drawn without its fences, beside a bar, and coloured by language when the grammar is one of the bundled ones; other code keeps one colour. This holds inside a list or a quote too. Top-level code also shows its language at the top right when there is room, and a line too long for the column continues on the next row. The comment box is 48 columns wide. `comment_width` changes that, down to a minimum of 38, and a narrower pane still narrows it: ```toml [ui] comment_width = 72 ``` The notes rail appears with a document review's first note and stays away while there are none. A code review decides as it opens: with notes the rail shows, without them it stays away until you open it, and a note saved later does not open it. `notes_rail` changes how a session starts: ```toml [ui] notes_rail = "when-notes" # default; or "shown" (always, notes or not) or "hidden" (closed) ``` `z` (`toggle-notes`) closes or opens the rail in the document and the code review alike, and the last choice is remembered in `clients/plannotator-tui/ui-state.json` under the data folder. A remembered choice wins over `notes_rail`, and one you left closed stays closed. A rail you left open shows from the start in the code review, notes or not, and saving a note there never opens or closes it. In a document, with `when-notes`, a rail remembered open still waits for the first note before it takes any columns. A mouse selection is copied to the clipboard when you release the button, in a document and in the code review (the selected lines' code). To leave the clipboard alone, as with Herdr's `ui.copy_on_select = false`, turn it off and press `y` on the selection when you want a copy: ```toml [ui] copy_on_select = false ``` ### How diffs open `[review]` sets how the code review draws its diff by default. Every key is optional, and a file without the table opens diffs as before: ```toml [review] layout = "auto" # auto (split in a terminal 141 columns wide or more; default) | split | unified split_ratio = 0.5 # the old side's share of a split row, 0.1 to 0.9; the new side gets the rest wrap = false # wrap long lines instead of scrolling them sideways notes = "panel" # panel (the notes panel only; default) | inline (boxes in the diff) | both line_numbers = true # line numbers in the gutter; off keeps the +/- signs theme = "auto" # the diff's colours: auto (follow [ui] theme, default) | dark | light background = "terminal" # terminal (the terminal's own background, default) | theme (the diff theme's) whitespace = "show" # show (default) | ignore-all (hide whitespace-only changes, like git diff -w) # | ignore-change (hide changes in the amount of whitespace, like git diff -b) tab_width = 4 # the columns a tab advances to, 1 to 16 (the menu offers 2, 4 and 8) inline_changes = "word" # changed text inside a line: word (default) | word-alt (as word, two changes # one character apart marked as one) | char | none (Pierre's lineDiffType names) ``` The app never writes this file. What you choose in the review (the settings menu, the header's switches, `u`, `w`, `W`, `(`/`)`, dragging the line between the sides) is remembered in `clients/plannotator-tui/review-settings.toml` under the data folder, and wins over `[review]` the next time; a key you never changed there keeps coming from `[review]`, then the defaults. **Reset to defaults**, the menu's last row, forgets the remembered choices. Each review writes only the keys it changed, so two reviews open at once keep each other's choices; a drag is remembered when you let go, to two decimals. If the remembered file cannot be read or written, the footer says so once and the review carries on with the settings it has. A bad value in `[review]` is an error like any other in the file: the review then opens with every default, and its footer says so once (`config not loaded: …; using defaults`), as the document screen does. A bad value in the remembered file is skipped and named once; its other keys still count. A remembered file that cannot be read at all (not UTF-8, say) is named once and replaced the next time a choice is remembered or Reset runs. `W` (or the menu's **Whitespace** row) hides the changes that only touch whitespace, as GitHub's "Hide whitespace" does, and `W` again shows them. While they are hidden, a lit `no ws` chip in the header says so; a click on it shows them again. Hidden, a removed line and an added line that differ only in whitespace are drawn as one unchanged line with both line numbers (unified, with the new text), and a hunk whose every change is like that shows only its heading, marked `whitespace only`. `W` hides as `-w` does unless you last chose `-b` in the menu, or `[review]` or the remembered choice says `ignore-change`. The diff works from the patch, not from the two files, so it differs from running `git diff -w`: lines pair only within one run of removed and added lines, a removed or added line with no partner (a blank one included) stays a change, a hunk with a real change keeps all its lines, and a file whose only changes are whitespace keeps its heading. The counts in the header and the file list stay those of the patch. Notes keep their lines: a note on a line drawn unchanged marks that row, a note in a hunk shown as its heading has no mark until the whitespace shows again (the rail says why when you pick it), and a comment written while whitespace is hidden is saved on the line and side it was written on. A selection keeps its lines when whitespace is hidden or shown, unless its hunk is now a heading alone; then it is cleared, and the footer says so. Go to definition opens a line hidden that way in the whole file. **Tab width** and **Changed text** (words; words, joined; characters; off) change how lines are drawn and marked, never which lines are shown. All three apply to the whole-file view too, where there are no changes to hide. `auto` decides by the terminal's width, never by the panes beside the diff, so saving a note, hiding or showing the file list or the notes, or dragging the lines between them never switches the layout under you; resizing the terminal decides again. A terminal of 141 columns or more splits: that leaves the diff 120 columns beside the file list at its narrowest, where the viewer's own auto splits a pane. A review of one file has no list and splits from 120 columns. Only a diff too narrow for two sides of 20 columns is drawn unified anyway. `split` and `unified` hold at any width. Each side of a split row keeps at least 20 columns, so on a narrow screen the line may sit nearer the middle than the ratio says. `(` and `)` move it in steps of 0.05 from the nearest step. The whole-file view is always unified. `theme` changes the diff only; the rest of the app keeps `[ui] theme`. ### Keys Every key is rebindable under `[keys]`: an action, and the keys that run it. ```toml [keys] left = ["j", "Left"] # jkl; instead of hjkl down = ["k", "Down"] up = ["l", "Up"] right = [";", "Right"] line-start = ["^", "Home"] ``` An entry replaces that action's keys and leaves every other action at its default; `[]` unbinds it. A key is one character (`G` is Shift+g), `ctrl+`, or one of `Up`, `Down`, `Left`, `Right`, `Home`, `End`, `PageUp`, `PageDown`, `Enter`, `Esc`, `Tab`, `Delete`, `Backspace`. An action keeps its meaning everywhere it applies, so `down` moves down in the document, the tree, the notes and every picker. A key bound to two actions that are live at the same time is an error that names both, and the hints at the bottom of the screen show your keys. `plannotator-tui config` prints every action with its keys. An explicit `--placement` or `PLANNOTATOR_TUI_PLACEMENT` still takes precedence. ## Rex Annotate Rex Annotate gives [Rex](https://www.superlogical.com/rex) the same reviews as Herdr Annotate: a key opens the focused pane's agent replies, its folder, its git changes, or its output in plannotator-tui, and **Send** makes the review the agent's next message: `Send 3 new ▸ claude in a1d6db (E)`. Rex has no plugin manifest, so Rex Annotate is a Lua module that Rex's config file loads. ```sh brew trust plannotator/tap && brew install plannotator/tap/plannotator-tui plannotator-tui rex install # writes ~/.config/rex/plannotator/annotate.lua ``` Add the line it prints to `~/.config/rex/init.lua`, then reload: ```lua require("plannotator.annotate").setup{} ``` ```sh rex config reload ``` `rex install` never edits `init.lua`. It writes the module beside it (in the folder of `$REX_CONFIG` when that is set), naming this binary by its full path, because Rex runs actions with a bare `PATH`. It then checks the module with `rex config check` against a scratch copy. Run it again after upgrading plannotator-tui. `--dry-run` says what it would write; `--print` writes the module to stdout instead. | Key | Action (`rex do …`, palette: Annotate) | Opens | |---|---|---| | `Shift+Cmd+O` | `annotate_last` | the agent's recent replies | | `Alt+Shift+Cmd+O` | `annotate_newest` | the agent's newest reply, with no picker | | `Ctrl+Cmd+O` | `annotate_open` | the pane's folder, with a file tree | | `Ctrl+Cmd+P` | `annotate_review_pick` | the [change picker](#pick-what-to-review) for the pane's repository | | | `annotate_gate` | the pane's folder, with **Approve** (`A`) | | | `annotate_terminal` | the pane's recent output | | | `annotate_find` | the newest `.md` file the pane's output names | | | `annotate_review` | a [code review](#code-review) of the uncommitted changes in the pane's repository | Rex for Mac binds none of these keys by default. Change or add keys, or bind none: ```lua require("plannotator.annotate").setup{ placement = "split", -- tab | split | popup; default: [rex] placement, else tab keys = { annotate_gate = "ctrl+cmd+a", annotate_last = false }, -- annotate_review_pick = false leaves Ctrl+Cmd+P alone; -- keys = false binds none; the actions stay in the palette } ``` A key you give any action in `keys` takes it from the default that had it: with `annotate_gate = "ctrl+cmd+p"`, Ctrl+Cmd+P opens the gate and the picker gets no key. A key you bind yourself with `rex.bind` wins when that line comes after `setup{}`. A review opens full size in a tab of its own, as Herdr's overlay does. It can open instead in a split to the right of the pane, so the agent stays in view, or in a floating popup over the pane's window: ```toml # ~/.config/plannotator-tui/config.toml [rex] placement = "tab" # tab (full size, default) | split | popup ``` The tab is a new tab (a Rex window) in the agent's session, named `Annotate · ` and the file, agent or folder it reviews. Send and `P` work as in a split. When the review ends, Rex closes its tab and plannotator-tui shows the pane it was opened from again, unless you have moved to another tab by then. Earlier releases opened a split by default; set `placement = "split"` to keep that. Everything goes through the Rex server, so the app's Remote Control setting can stay off. ### Launchers The actions run these, and so can a script or an agent. Each opens the review and exits: ```sh plannotator-tui rex last [--newest] # the agent's replies plannotator-tui rex open [file.md | folder] # a document, or the pane's folder plannotator-tui rex terminal [--lines N] # the pane's recent output; --print writes it out plannotator-tui rex find [--lines N] # the newest .md file the pane's output names plannotator-tui rex review [--staged | --unstaged | --base REF | --commit SHA | PR | --pick] # a code review of the pane's repository ``` The pane is `--block `, else `REX_BLOCK`, so an agent that runs a launcher in its own shell reviews itself; that is how it hands you a plan. `--placement split|popup|tab` overrides the config. `--paste` puts the feedback in the agent's prompt without pressing Enter and focuses the agent's pane, so you can edit it first; the header says `claude prompt in a1d6db`. `rex open --gate [--result-file ]` adds Approve for a sign-off, as `herdr open --gate` does. `rex review` reviews the git repository of the pane's folder, as `herdr review` does: a folder that is not in a repository, or a scope you named with no changes to review, fails before any split opens, and `--pick` (or no scope with nothing to review) opens the change picker. Code review is not available on Windows yet. Send goes to the agent in the pane the review was opened from, with no question asked. `P` lists every other agent Rex runs, in every session and window, the ones in the review's own window first, so a review opened from one agent can go to another (see [Choosing the agent](#choosing-the-agent)). A review you start yourself in a Rex pane, with no launcher, asks which agent on the first Send. The agent is the one the pane's program reports to Rex (its program status app, such as `pi` or `claude-code`), else the one its process is named after. So pi, which runs under `node`, gets Send like any other agent. A pane with no agent copies instead. A send waits while Rex reports the agent blocked on a permission prompt or a question, as it does in Herdr: nothing is sent or copied, the notes stay pending, and `E` retries. It also needs the agent to report its state to Rex (Claude Code, Codex and pi do): until it has, the review copies instead, since Enter could answer a dialog Rex cannot see, and `--paste` still works. Rex does not report its theme to programs, so with a light Rex theme set `[ui] theme = "light"`. ## Inside herdr-core [herdr-core](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-core) (`hc`) runs the terminals and [herdr-app](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app) is its window. Neither has Herdr's plugins, so plannotator-tui is started by a command rather than a manifest. Run it in an hc terminal: ```sh plannotator-tui hc last [--newest] [--session ] # the agent's replies plannotator-tui hc open [file.md | folder] # a document, or the terminal's folder plannotator-tui hc open plan.md --gate [--result-file ] # adds Approve, as `herdr open --gate` plannotator-tui hc review [--staged | --unstaged | --base REF | --commit SHA | PR | --pick] # a code review of the terminal's repository ``` Each starts plannotator-tui in a terminal of its own, `annotate-`, and shows it in herdr-app: over the tab for `overlay` and `popup` (the default), or in a pane beside the focused one for `split`, from `--placement` or `[herdr] placement`. The review starts once herdr-app shows it: until herdr-app tells a new terminal its colours, the terminal answers a colour query with the core's dark default, so asking sooner would draw a dark palette on a light window. herdr-app needs a moment to learn of a new terminal, so the launcher asks again for up to 3 s while it answers "no running terminal"; any other refusal, or no herdr-app window at all, ends that at once. Then the review starts anyway and cannot know your colours: the launcher prints herdr-app's reason and the `hc attach` command. Set `[ui] theme` for that case. The terminal is removed when the review ends, and hc does not type a note about it into the agent's prompt. One review per terminal at a time. `hc review` reviews the git repository of the terminal's folder, as `herdr review` does: a folder that is not in a repository, or a scope you named with no changes to review, fails before any terminal starts, and `--pick` (or no scope with nothing to review) opens the change picker. The terminal is `--terminal ` (an address or a name), else `HC_TERMINAL_ID`, so an agent that runs a launcher in its own terminal reviews itself; that is how it hands you a plan. The header button sends the review to the agent as its next message with `hc send`: `Send 3 new ▸ pi in t7 (E)`. A terminal with no agent copies instead. A send needs the agent to still be the terminal's foreground program and to have reported its state to hc (OSC 7501), because Enter could answer a dialog hc cannot see. `hc send` also refuses an agent that reports it is blocked, and the review says so; nothing is copied and `E` retries. hc has no exact session for an agent, so `hc last` reads the newest transcript in the agent's folder. Another agent in that folder may have written one more recently; `--session` names the right transcript. Terminals on another machine and `terminal` reviews (a terminal's recent output) are not supported yet. The feedback travels as one argument to `hc send`, so the OS caps its size (128 KiB on Linux, about 1 MiB on macOS). A longer review is not sent: the review copies it instead and says why. ## Choosing the agent `P` (`pick-target`) opens a picker of every agent Send can reach, in document and code reviews alike: - running Pi sessions with the [Pi extension](#pi); - inside Herdr, every pane with an agent (Claude, Codex, Pi and the rest), named by agent, folder, state, and `workspace › tab · pane`, so two Claude panes are told apart. The review's own pane is never listed. - inside Rex, every pane with an agent in every Rex session and window (tab), named by agent, folder, state, and `session › window · pane`. A pane you gave a label shows it (`claude · reviewer`); otherwise the row shows the title the agent set, such as the task Claude Code is on (`claude · Fix login redirect`). An agent that has not reported its state to Rex reads `no state`; Send refuses it, as it does for a launcher (see [Rex Annotate](#rex-annotate)). A Pi session in a Rex pane is one row, sent to over the Pi link and placed where Rex has it. The review's own pane is never listed. ``` ╭ send to which agent? ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ claude · Fix login redirect ~/work/api idle work › api · 9ba798 │ │ codex ~/work/api/src working work › api · 31496a │ │ claude · Migrate styles ~/work/web blocked work › web · 63239c │ │ claude · release ~/work/notes idle side › Window 122adf3e · fd82e9 │ │ pi · π - notes ~/work/notes idle work › web · eda7cc │ ╰ ↑↓ move · enter send here · esc close ────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ ``` Inside Rex, the agents in the review's own window come first. Then agents in the review's folder, then by name; the rows do not move while the picker is open. In a narrow pane the folders are shortened first, so the state and the place stay in view. The pick becomes the Send target until you change it, and the last row goes back to the target the review started with. Launched from an agent (a Herdr, Rex or herdr-core launcher, or `--deliver-to`), Send goes to that agent and `P` switches. Launched on its own, with no [delivery command](#any-other-agent-a-delivery-command), Send opens the picker whenever an agent is within reach, and the button says `Send 1 new ▸ choose agent (E)`. `Enter` sends to the agent under the cursor (the first one) and keeps it as the target; `Copy to clipboard`, one row up, copies this once; `Esc` sends nothing. With no agent within reach, Send copies as before. herdr-core agents are reached only through their launcher. ## Pi plannotator-tui can send a review to any running [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) session, and Pi can leave notes in the file you have open. Install the extension once: ```sh plannotator-tui pi install # copies it into ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ ``` Restart your Pi sessions, or run `/reload` in each one. Run `plannotator-tui pi install` again after upgrading plannotator-tui: the binary does not notice an older extension, and some fixes need the new one (for example, `last` following Pi's place after `/tree`). Then: - **Send to a Pi:** press `P` (`pick-target`) to choose a session (see [Choosing the agent](#choosing-the-agent)). Send (`E`) then goes to that session, as a user message. A busy Pi reads it once its current work is done. - **Notes from Pi:** Pi gets a `plannotator_tui_note` tool. It quotes text from a file you have open, optionally with a line number, and its note shows up beside that text marked `pi · `. The note is sent with the rest of your review. - **Review from Pi:** `/plannotator-review` runs `plannotator-tui review --pick` in Pi's own terminal. Pi's screen steps aside, you [pick what to review](#pick-what-to-review) in the session's folder, and Send goes back to that session; Pi's screen returns when the review quits, also when Pi is told to end while the review runs (the review ends with it). If the review cannot find that Pi session when you Send, it says so and copies the feedback instead of sending it to any other pane. `PLANNOTATOR_TUI_BIN` names the binary, else `plannotator-tui` on `PATH`. - `plannotator-tui pi list` lists the sessions; `plannotator-tui pi send --session ` sends stdin to one. Each side lists itself in `clients/plannotator-tui/sessions/` in the data folder (see below) and listens on 127.0.0.1 with a secret token; nothing leaves this computer. The protocol is in [`docs/spec-pi-link.md`](docs/spec-pi-link.md) and the extension in [`integrations/pi/`](integrations/pi/). ## Any other agent: a delivery command Herdr, Rex and herdr-core are built in. For anything else, such as tmux, a script or another agent's CLI, name a command that takes the feedback on stdin: ```sh export PLANNOTATOR_TUI_DELIVER_CMD='tmux load-buffer - && tmux paste-buffer -p -t agent && tmux send-keys -t agent Enter' ``` or, for every review: ```toml # ~/.config/plannotator-tui/config.toml [deliver] command = "~/bin/send-to-agent" ``` The environment variable wins over the config. Send (`E`) then runs the command and the header names it by its first word: `Send 3 new ▸ cmd · tmux (E)`. - **How it runs:** the value is one command line for the shell: `sh -c` on macOS and Linux, `cmd /S /C` on Windows. Pipelines, `&&` and variables work. The feedback is on stdin, the same text `E` would copy. `PLANNOTATOR_TUI_REVIEW_PATH` is the file or folder under review, when the review opened one, and the command inherits the review's environment. - **The exit status is the outcome:** | Exit | Means | The review | |---|---|---| | `0` | delivered | marks the notes sent; the first line on stdout, if any, joins the status | | `75` | the agent cannot take a message now, e.g. it is at a dialog | keeps the notes pending and copies nothing; `E` retries | | `69` | there is no agent to send to | copies the feedback; `E` retries | | anything else | the send failed | shows the first line of stderr; `E` retries | 75 and 69 are `EX_TEMPFAIL` and `EX_UNAVAILABLE` from `sysexits.h`. The first line of stderr (else stdout) says why in the status. - **It should be quick.** The review waits for the command and stops it after 30 s. A child it leaves running in the background (`cmd &`) does not hold the review up. - **Where it sits:** a target that a Herdr, Rex or herdr-core launcher named for this review comes first, because it names one agent for one review. The command replaces the clipboard everywhere else. A gated review (`--gate`) with no launcher still gives its decision to whoever ran it, and `P` can still switch Send to another agent. For Pi, `plannotator-tui pi send` is already such a command (see [Pi](#pi)): ```sh PLANNOTATOR_TUI_DELIVER_CMD='plannotator-tui pi send --session my-session' plannotator-tui plan.md ``` If that session has closed, or no session matches, `pi send` exits 69, so the review copies the feedback instead. ## Agent replies `plannotator-tui last` finds the transcript of the agent that launched your shell and shows a picker of its recent replies. Hosts: Claude Code, Codex, pi, Oh My Pi, GitHub Copilot CLI, Droid, Hermes CLI, OpenCode (1 and 2), Command Code (`cmd`), Antigravity CLI (`agy`). `--host`, `--pid`, `--session ` (format sniffed when no host is named) and `--session-id ` (Hermes, OpenCode) override detection; `--stdin` reads a document; `--newest` skips the picker and opens the newest reply straight away, with `p` still opening the picker on the rest; the picker offers the 25 newest replies, or as many as `pick` under `[last]` in the config file says, also inside Herdr and Rex, and `--pick N` for one run; `--print` writes the newest reply to stdout and always exits 0 (for hooks and scripts). A reply review keeps its annotations in memory only; nothing about it survives the run, but the feedback you send or copy is archived like any other (see Feedback archive below). On Linux, an explicit Codex `--pid` selects the rollout opened by that process. If it cannot be identified uniquely, `last` reports the failure instead of choosing an unrelated session. `--session` and `--session-id` keep precedence over PID discovery. Inside Herdr, the exact-session path needs the session id Herdr reports for the pane. Herdr's Claude Code integration registers on `SessionStart`, so a session reports its id only when it started after `herdr integration install claude`; a session that was already running when the integration was installed reports none. Without an id, `last` shows the newest transcript for the folder, which is a guess when several sessions share one directory, and says so in the status line. ## Where annotations live ``` ~/.plannotator/clients/plannotator-tui/annotations///annotations.json ``` `` is the git repo name, `` the file's basename plus 8 hex of the sha256 of its path: Plannotator's own layout, so both tools see one record per file. The JSON is the Plannotator Workspaces wire shape; any agent can read it. Nothing is written next to your files. `PLANNOTATOR_DATA_DIR` relocates the directory. ### Feedback archive A successful Send or Copy also appends what was submitted (the feedback text, the quoted selections and their annotations, and the file, folder or agent session it was about) to `{data_dir}/feedback//index.jsonl`, with a Markdown copy under `records/`. The data dir is `PLANNOTATOR_DATA_DIR`, else an existing `~/.plannotator`, else `$XDG_DATA_HOME/plannotator`, else `~/.plannotator`. File, folder and reply reviews are all archived; a send that fails or is refused is not. The format is the one the Plannotator browser app writes, so both tools share one history. To turn it off, set `PLANNOTATOR_FEEDBACK_HISTORY=0` (once the variable is set, only `1` or `true` enable) or put `"feedbackHistory": false` in `{data_dir}/config.json`; the variable wins over the file. ## Headless ```sh plannotator-tui --export # all active notes, to stdout (no delivery recorded) plannotator-tui --annotate [comment|looks_good|delete] [--occurrence N] plannotator-tui --snapshot [cols rows scroll] [quote] # one frame as text plannotator-tui --bench # parse / layout timings plannotator-tui herdr terminal [--lines N] --print # a Herdr pane's recent output as a document ``` ## Repository - `crates/plannotator-tui`: the app. `crates/plannotator-tui-schema`: annotation and anchor types, wire-compatible with Plannotator Workspaces. `crates/plannotator-tui-hosts`: agent transcript readers. - `docs/decisions.md` is the design record; `AGENTS.md` the engineering rules; `crates/plannotator-tui/README.md` the full key reference and measurements.
